# Orange-throated Warbler, Orange-throated Warbler

Blackburnian Warbler. Dendroica fusca.

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [University Park](https://www.eafit.edu.co/universidad-parque)
- [Biotic Inventory](https://www.eafit.edu.co/universidad-parque/inventario-biotico)
- Orange-throated Warbler

[![Image of an Orange-throated Warbler](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/d5e70d2d-e2be-465d-80e8-a93cf771e71e/web/reinita-gargantianaranja.webp)](https://www.eafit.edu.co/universidad-parque/inventario-biotico/reinita-gargantianaranja)

![](https://www.eafit.edu.co/universidad-parque/inventario-biotico/reinita-gargantianaranja)

###### Etymology

Dendroica, from the Greek dendron, tree; oikos, dwelling, house. Fusca, from the Latin fuscus, dark coloration, brown.

###### Description

A small bird, 13 cm long, with a slender appearance. Breeding plumage: the male is mainly black above, with two white lines on the back; ventrally, the throat and breast are deep reddish-orange; the lower breast and abdomen are white with black streaks on the sides; the head has a small patch on the crown and yellow sides; the supercilium descends behind the ear coverts, and the malar stripe is black, forming a small mask; the wings are black with an extensive white patch on the wing coverts; the tail is black with the outer rectrices spotted with white. The female has a similar color pattern to the male, but above is grayish with dark streaking; the throat, breast, crown, and sides of the head are yellow to pale orange; the flanks are greenish-gray. Non-breeding plumage: the male has the same plumage pattern as the breeding male, but is generally duller, above is olive-black, the orange is less intense or replaced by pale yellow, and there are prominent white wing bars. The female is dull olive-green above with paler wing bars.

###### Ecology

It inhabits mature coniferous and mixed forests in North America. It winters in montane, premontane, and dry forests in Central and South America, though it also frequents woodland patches and gardens. It generally forages alone and occasionally in pairs or groups, searching for insects in the middle and upper levels of the canopy, often within mixed flocks. It nests in trees, usually on conifer branches, where it constructs an open cup of twigs, pine needles, cobwebs, bark, plant fibers, moss, and hair. They lay three to five greenish-white eggs with brown spots and blotches.

###### Distribution

A boreal migrant that winters in the Andes. It breeds in Canada and the United States. During the winter, it is distributed mainly from northern Venezuela to Bolivia. In the Colombian Andes, it is the most common migratory warbler. It is observed from September to May, from sea level up to 3600 m. During migration, it is relatively common foraging in the canopy of trees such as eucalyptus (Eucalyptus sp.), Gualanday (Jacaranda mimosifolia), and Yellow Acacia (Caesalpinia peltophoroides) on the EAFIT University campus.
